source: Built from the C202 Ch 1-14 decks and study guides (Phillips, Human Resource Management, 3rd ed.)
summary:
# C202 final quiz: review deck

A short review of the C202 final quiz (all 14 chapters). There's one test-style question for each quiz concept, reworded so you learn the idea instead of memorizing the wording. After those come a few related practice questions aimed at your flagged weak spots. Progress here is separate from the chapter decks, but every answer also counts toward the weak-spot tracker for the matching section, and the copied cards count toward their chapter originals.

Rounds are 20 questions, so this is about three rounds.

cards.front: A CEO asks what HR's biggest contribution to carrying out company strategy should be. What's the best answer?
choices: Running safety training on a yearly schedule
Posting the employee handbook where everyone can find it
Applying discipline and terminations the same way for everyone
Bringing in, growing, and keeping the strongest talent the strategy needs
cards.explanation: People carry out strategy, so HR adds the most strategic value by acquiring, developing, and retaining top talent. The other choices are routine administrative tasks.
cards.subtitle: Final review · HR and strategy
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy

cards.front: A firm shifts from cheap mass production to custom, high-touch service. What should most shape how it now moves people into, through, and out of the company?
cards.explanation: The business strategy (where and how the firm competes) sets how it treats employees and how it manages the flow of people in, within, and out. Sales, marketing, and financial plans support the strategy; they don't define HR's direction.
cards.subtitle: Final review · HR and strategy
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy

cards.front: Which HR effort most directly raises a company's overall organizational performance?
choices: Studying which new products the market wants
Building the company's ability to handle growth and change
Rewriting the company's mission and vision statement
Coaching executives on investment and financing choices
cards.explanation: HR boosts performance through people: making the workforce adaptable so the firm can absorb growth and change. Finance, product research, and mission-writing belong to other functions. HR also supports leadership by offering professional development and growth.
cards.subtitle: Final review · HR and performance
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: Company policy requires business casual dress. A manager immediately fires every employee who ignores it. Legally, what has the manager done?
choices: Nothing illegal: at-will employees can be fired for breaking a neutral policy
Broken the law by firing without a warning first
Violated the employees' right to free expression
cards.explanation: Under employment at will, an employer can end employment for any lawful reason, and violating a neutral, job-related policy is lawful. Progressive discipline is good practice but not required by law.
cards.subtitle: Final review · At-will employment

cards.front: A worker says she was never paid time-and-a-half for her 50-hour weeks and earns less than the federal minimum. Which law covers this?
cards.explanation: The FLSA sets the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and child-labor rules. The NLRA covers unions, the EPA covers sex-based pay gaps, and WARN covers layoff notice.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Employment laws
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A manufacturer with 4,000 workers plans to cut 800 jobs at one plant next quarter. Which law creates specific obligations for it?
choices: Equal Pay Act: equal severance for men and women
WARN Act: 60 days' advance notice of the mass layoff
National Labor Relations Act: a vote before any layoff
Fair Labor Standards Act: final paychecks within 24 hours
cards.explanation: The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (1988) requires employers with 100+ full-time workers to give 60 days' notice of plant closings and mass layoffs.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Employment laws
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: Under which law are two jobs 'equal' if they need substantially the same skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions at the same site?
choices: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
cards.explanation: The EPA requires equal pay for men and women doing equal work, defined by skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions in the same establishment.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Employment laws
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A 45-year-old applicant, born in Denver and fluent in English and French, is passed over for a job he's qualified for. Which protected class is most likely at issue?
cards.explanation: The ADEA protects people 40 and older, so age is the protected trait here. A U.S.-born applicant points away from national origin, and language alone isn't a listed class. (On the quiz, a 37-year-old didn't qualify for age protection, so gender was the answer.)
cards.subtitle: Final review · Protected classes
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A supervisor hints that staff who go out with him will get the best shifts and those who refuse won't. What kind of harassment is this?
cards.explanation: Quid pro quo ('this for that') ties job benefits or threats to sexual favors and usually involves someone with power over the victim. Hostile environment is pervasive unwelcome conduct with no exchange.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Sexual harassment
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: A company makes only applicants of one ethnicity show a U.S. diploma to prove their English, and doesn't ask anyone else. What type of discrimination is this?
cards.explanation: Holding one protected group to a different requirement is intentional, unequal treatment: disparate treatment. Adverse impact is when the same rule for everyone ends up hurting one group more.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Disparate treatment
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: Every applicant for a nursing job faces the same requirements, yet far fewer men than women get hired. What might the men be experiencing?
cards.explanation: Adverse impact happens when a rule that applies equally to everyone screens out a protected group at a much higher rate. Disparate treatment would mean the men faced different rules.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Adverse impact
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: Which order is essentially the source of affirmative action, requiring federal contractors to set hiring goals for women and minorities?
choices: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
cards.explanation: Executive Order 11246 requires federal contractors to take affirmative steps to integrate their workforces, including written plans and goals. Title VII bans discrimination but doesn't require those plans.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Affirmative action

cards.front: Which is a legitimate way for a company to practice affirmative action?
choices: Limiting succession programs to minority employees
Offering signing bonuses only to protected-class applicants
Promoting minority employees even when they are less qualified
Recruiting at colleges with large minority student populations
cards.explanation: Affirmative action widens the applicant pool through outreach; final decisions still have to be merit-based. Quotas, reserved programs, or bonuses limited to one group are themselves discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Affirmative action

cards.front: A shop owner thinks affirmative action means she must hire someone from a minority group, so she picks an applicant based on how she looks. What is her belief an example of?
cards.explanation: Her mistake is about what the law requires (affirmative action doesn't force small businesses to hire by race), so it is ignorance. Ignorance is never a legal defense, and it feeds stereotyping, which applies a generalization (even a 'positive' one) to everyone in a group.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Human biases

cards.front: Managers find that salespeople spend most of their week on paperwork unrelated to selling. Before reassigning tasks, which HR tool should they use to study the job?
cards.explanation: Job analysis systematically identifies a job's tasks and the traits needed to do it well. Its findings guide redesign. Enlargement, enrichment, and rotation are design choices that come afterward.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Job analysis

cards.front: On a new hire's first day, a coworker explains who reports to whom, who to ask when she's stuck, and how decisions get made. What is he describing?
cards.explanation: Organizational structure is the formal system of tasks, power, and reporting relationships. The chart is only a diagram of it. Organizational design is choosing and adjusting that structure to meet goals.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Organizational structure

cards.front: A company announces that all full-time employees get two weeks of paid vacation each year. What has it created?
cards.explanation: A policy is a guiding principle, a decision already made. A procedure is the steps to follow (how to request the time off), and a rule is a specific must or must-not. Policies, procedures, and rules together support the organizational structure.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Policies, procedures, rules

cards.front: A company wants new hires who will strengthen its culture. What should it focus on most when evaluating applicants?
cards.explanation: Culture is shared values and norms, so hiring for culture (person-organization fit) means assessing values and integrity. Skills and experience speak to person-job fit.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Fit

cards.front: A team lead is bored by her work, dislikes motivating people, and dreads giving reviews, though she likes the company and her team. Which fit is poor?
cards.explanation: Her problem is the job's demands and rewards, not the team or the company, so person-job fit is the mismatch.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Fit

cards.front: An employee thinks a promotion was decided before interviews began, since the manager had a quiet favorite. Which fairness is she questioning?
cards.explanation: Procedural fairness is about whether the process was consistent and unbiased. Distributive fairness concerns the outcome itself, and interactional fairness concerns how respectfully people were treated.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Fairness perceptions

cards.front: At the end of each interview, a director asks manager candidates how they would bring down quitting rates in their department. What type of question is this?
cards.explanation: Case questions give the candidate a real business problem to analyze and solve. Behavioral questions ask about past actions ('describe a tough problem you solved'), so they test skills, not motivation. Situational questions pose a hypothetical moment for one person.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Interview types
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A recruiter tracks industry trends and where skilled candidates are, then reaches out to promising people about an opening. What is she doing?
cards.explanation: Sourcing finds potential candidates and talent pools. Recruiting then persuades them to become applicants. She's doing sourcing first, then recruiting.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Sourcing and recruiting

cards.front: An executive moving to Japan needs to learn how to work effectively with Japanese colleagues. Which training fits best?
cards.explanation: Culture-specific training targets one country or culture. General cross-cultural training builds broad cultural awareness that isn't tied to any one place.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Cross-cultural training
cards.note: Read more: 7.15 Training in Ethics, Global Leadership, and Diversity

cards.front: A diversity program follows the usual training steps: assess needs, set objectives, design, then the next step. What comes fourth?
choices: Check whether discrimination claims went down
Agree on the session dates and locations
Deliver the training, starting with senior managers
Decide whether a new policy would work better than training
cards.explanation: The training process runs needs assessment, objectives, design, implementation, evaluation. Step four is implementation. Measuring the drop in claims is evaluation, and weighing a policy instead is part of needs assessment.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Diversity training
cards.note: Read more: 7.15 Training in Ethics, Global Leadership, and Diversity

cards.front: Which of these is NOT one of the sensory modalities (learning styles)?
cards.explanation: The sensory modalities are visual, auditory, tactile, and kinesthetic. 'Experiential' is a training method (role plays, simulations), not a learning style.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Learning styles
cards.note: Read more: 7.9 Design the Training Program: Games to Learning Styles

cards.front: A hospital compares patient satisfaction scores from before and after its nurse training. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
cards.explanation: Patient or customer satisfaction is a business outcome, so it's the results level. Reaction is how the trainees felt about the training (the trap you fell for on the Q2 quiz).
cards.subtitle: Final review · Kirkpatrick levels
cards.note: Read more: 7.12 Evaluate the Training: Kirkpatrick's Model and Return on Investment

cards.front: How should employee performance goals be written to get the best results?
cards.explanation: Specific, difficult goals produce higher performance than easy or vague 'do your best' goals.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Goal setting
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A supervisor rates only the parts of an employee's work she has actually seen. Which concept is this about?
cards.explanation: Task acquaintance is the amount and type of work contact a rater has with the person being rated. Accurate raters stick to what they've observed.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Performance information

cards.front: Coworkers tend to rate each other most honestly when the ratings will be used for what?
cards.explanation: Peers inflate or soften ratings when they affect a colleague's pay, promotion, or discipline. When ratings only feed development, they're more candid.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Performance information

cards.front: A manager rates an employee 'average' only because the rest of the team is exceptional, without checking the job's actual standards. Which error is this?
cards.explanation: The contrast effect rates people against each other instead of against set standards. Halo and horns let one trait color every rating, and recency over-weights the latest events.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Rating errors
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors

cards.front: Which progressive discipline step is informal and doesn't have to be documented?
cards.explanation: Counseling is an informal conversation that flags the problem early. Written warnings, suspensions, and terminations are documented formal steps.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Progressive discipline

cards.front: Which practice most increases both inclusion and engagement?
choices: Letting employees use their unique skills and strengths
Limiting how much decision authority employees have
cards.explanation: People feel included and engaged when their unique abilities are valued and used. The other choices reduce autonomy, feedback, and growth.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Inclusion
cards.note: Read more: 3.6 The Importance of Diversity and Inclusion to Business Performance

cards.front: Unemployment is at a record low and the economy is booming. Which departure should HR expect to rise?
choices: Employees quitting for better-paying jobs elsewhere
cards.explanation: A strong economy with plenty of jobs makes voluntary turnover rise because people have options. Firings and eliminated jobs are involuntary turnover, which the employer starts.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Turnover

cards.front: A star performer asks for a modest raise, hears raises happen only at the annual review, and quits. What kind of turnover is this?
cards.explanation: Losing a high performer the firm wanted to keep is dysfunctional turnover, and it was avoidable. Functional turnover is when low performers leave.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Turnover

cards.front: Which is an INDIRECT cost when an employee quits?
choices: Lower morale among the coworkers who stay
cards.explanation: Indirect costs are hidden effects such as lost morale, heavier workloads, and lost knowledge. Training, advertising, and hiring fees are direct costs.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Cost of turnover

cards.front: Which retention tactic works as a mobility barrier?
choices: Training employees deeply in the company's own unique methods
Writing job ads that oversell the role
cards.explanation: Mobility barriers make leaving harder. Firm-specific skills, like unvested stock, are worth less elsewhere, so they lower the chance employees leave.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Retention

cards.front: Which is NOT a benefit of succession management?
choices: Fewer premature promotions and long vacancies
Smoother transitions when key people leave
cards.explanation: Succession management keeps ready candidates for key roles. That gives leadership continuity, smooth transitions, and fewer long vacancies or rushed promotions. It also shows employees a growth path, which helps retention. It doesn't by itself reduce discrimination risk.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Succession management

cards.front: Which is an example of workforce redeployment?
choices: Hiring contractors to handle supply swings
Moving employees with specialized expertise onto a critical project
Laying off staff when a branch closes
Letting top-rated employees work from home
cards.explanation: Redeployment moves existing talent to where it's needed most instead of laying people off or hiring outside.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Redeploying talent

cards.front: Facing budget cuts, a manager weighs canceling all 30 employees' holiday bonuses against laying off five part-timers, choosing whichever does the least overall harm. Which ethical standard is she using?
cards.explanation: The utilitarian standard picks the option that produces the most good and the least harm overall. Rights protects individual entitlements, and fairness asks whether people are treated equally.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Ethical standards
cards.note: Read more: 2.7 The Role of HRM in Corporate Ethics and Social Responsibility

cards.front: Which of these is an ethical issue in HR?
choices: Building interest in a wellness program
Deciding how to respond to a bullying complaint
cards.explanation: Ethical issues involve right-and-wrong choices that affect people's well-being, like how to handle a bullying claim. The others are routine operations.
cards.subtitle: Final review · HR ethics
cards.note: Read more: 2.8 Ethical and Unethical Behavior

cards.front: Which culture type stresses internal harmony, spreads power among all members, and depends on group morale?
cards.explanation: Consensual cultures value loyalty, tradition, and harmony, with power shared across the group. Competitive cultures focus on winning, entrepreneurial ones on risk and innovation, and bureaucratic ones on rules and procedures.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Culture types
cards.note: Read more: 2.4 Why Is Organizational Culture Important?

cards.front: Two companies are merging this year. Which is a key HR job?
choices: Setting the merged company's business strategy
Planning for talent and retaining key people
cards.explanation: In mergers, HR's role is talent: deciding who's needed, keeping key employees, and combining cultures. Suppliers, financial forecasts, and strategy belong to other leaders.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Mergers
cards.note: Read more: 2.13 HRM During Mergers and Acquisitions

cards.front: Why should a pay system's rewards be closely tied to company objectives?
choices: People guess at what management wants
People do whatever is most convenient
People tend to repeat whatever gets measured and rewarded
cards.explanation: Rewards signal what matters. Employees repeat rewarded behavior, so pay should reward the behaviors the strategy needs.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Strategic compensation

cards.front: A chain will send its single top-selling store manager on a luxury trip. What will this contest probably do?
choices: Increase teamwork among the store managers
Raise morale at historically weak stores
Keep and motivate the managers who think they have a real shot at winning
cards.explanation: A winner-take-all individual incentive motivates the people who think they can win. It can hurt cooperation and discourage managers at weak stores who have little chance.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Incentive plans

cards.front: An employer raises its 401(k) match, adds financial-planning seminars, and offers long-term care insurance. What goal is it pursuing?
cards.explanation: Retirement savings, planning help, and long-term care coverage all target employees' security in retirement.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Benefits
cards.note: Read more: 11.4 What Is the Purpose of Benefits?

cards.front: Which benefit is NOT legally required of U.S. employers?
cards.explanation: Social Security, unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and FMLA leave are mandatory. Dropping workers' comp would violate employee rights. Health insurance is a customary benefit, not a universal legal requirement. Workers' comp is no-fault: an employee qualifies just by having a work-related injury or illness.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Mandatory benefits

cards.front: An employee feels overwhelmed and isn't sure he can keep up with his job. What is he most likely experiencing?
cards.explanation: Too many demands for too long is dysfunctional stress, which is linked to withdrawal and turnover. Functional stress is the manageable, energizing kind (satisfaction, excitement), though it can still turn counterproductive if anxiety goes unmanaged. The turnover options describe people leaving, not stress.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Stress

cards.front: Many employers have kept workers from unionizing by investing in which relationship factor?
cards.explanation: When the unwritten expectations between employer and employees (the psychological contract) are met, workers feel less need for a union.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Labor relations
cards.note: Read more: 13.14 Establishing Positive Labor-Management Relations

cards.front: Which statement is true?
choices: Employment at will lets an employer fire anyone for any reason at all
Handling cash with the public doesn't affect violence risk
OSHA rules cover only employers with ten or more workers
The Taft-Hartley Act banned closed shops and secondary boycotts
cards.explanation: Taft-Hartley (1947) added union unfair labor practices and outlawed closed shops and secondary boycotts. At-will still has legal limits, OSHA covers nearly all private employers, and handling cash is a known violence risk.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Labor law

cards.front: Which is NOT a union tactic for pressuring management during bargaining?
cards.explanation: A lockout is a management tactic: the employer keeps workers out. Strikes, boycotts, and slowdowns are union pressure tactics.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Negotiation breakdowns

cards.front: In a unionized company that must cut jobs, what usually decides who is laid off first?
cards.explanation: Union contracts usually make seniority the key factor: last in, first out.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Unions and HR
cards.note: Read more: 13.13 How Unions Impact Human Resource Management

cards.front: Which HR function makes sure what individual employees aim for lines up with what the organization is trying to achieve?
cards.explanation: Performance management aligns employee goals and behavior with organizational goals, then appraises and improves performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q8 · Effective HRM

cards.front: Which of these is an ethical dilemma in HRM?
choices: A manager asks HR to quietly drop a qualified applicant after learning he's in cancer treatment
A manager schedules quarterly career conversations
HR chooses between two strong internal candidates using posted criteria
HR moves open enrollment to November
cards.explanation: A dilemma involves pressure to do something unfair or harmful. Picking fairly between good candidates is hard but not unethical.
cards.subtitle: Ch 2.8 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 2.8 Ethical and Unethical Behavior

cards.front: A posting reads: 'Schedules patient appointments, verifies insurance, and reports to the clinic manager. Some Saturdays required.' What document is this drawn from?
cards.explanation: Duties, reporting relationships, and special conditions are the content of a job description.
cards.subtitle: Ch 4.14 Apply · Effective HRM

cards.front: Employees using emergency time must call their supervisor within one hour of their shift start. This statement is a...
cards.explanation: Likely per text: it tells employees how to carry out the policy, which makes it a procedure.
cards.subtitle: Ch 4 Quiz Q19 · Effective HRM

cards.front: A month later, supervisors observe that Kai now uses the new safety checklist correctly on every shift. Which level is this?
cards.explanation: Applying learning on the job (transfer) is the behavior level.
cards.subtitle: Ch 7.12 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 7.12 Evaluate the Training: Kirkpatrick's Model and Return on Investment

cards.front: Why is feedback important?
choices: It creates more chances for discipline
cards.explanation: Likely per text: feedback tracks progress toward goals so people can adjust.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8 Quiz Q7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: Which two progressive discipline steps may an employer repeat?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: written warning and suspension. Moderate confidence: the text explicitly says only that the written warning may repeat (the second becomes a final warning); 'counseling and written warning' is the main alternative.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8 Quiz Q10 · Effective HRM

cards.front: A sales team's two lowest performers quit on their own, and the firm easily hires stronger replacements. How is this turnover best described?
cards.explanation: They chose to leave (voluntary), and losing low performers who are easy to replace helps the company (functional).
cards.subtitle: Final review · Turnover

cards.front: A strength test passes 80% of male applicants but only 40% of female applicants. What does the four-fifths rule suggest?
choices: No problem, unless fewer than 100 people applied
Possible adverse impact, since 40% is less than 80% of the men's rate
Disparate treatment, because women were singled out
No problem, because the same test was given to everyone
cards.explanation: If a group's pass rate is under four-fifths (80%) of the top group's rate, that's evidence of adverse impact. Here 40/80 = 50%. The employer would then have to show the test is job-related.
cards.subtitle: Final review · Adverse impact
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
